s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: organ in the mouth used for speaking and eating
s.c: Though in ⟦James 3:5|James 3:5⟧ the tongue is referred to as a part of the body, it is used essentially as a symbol for speech, and since in some languages the tongue is not regarded as an organ of speech, but simply as a part of the mouth, it may be necessary to change the expression to read ‘the mouth is a small member of the body’ or ‘speaking is only a small part of one’s life.’ It is obviously not the tongue as an organ which corrupts the whole person, but the capacity for speech which has such a corrupting effect.

s.d: a language, with the possible implication of its distinctive form
s.c: The miracle described in ⟦Acts 2:4|Acts 2:4⟧ may have been a miracle of speaking or a miracle of hearing, but at any rate people understood fully, and therefore it seems appropriate in this context to speak of ‘languages’ in contrast with ⟦1 Corinthians 14:2|1 Corinthians 14:2⟧, in which case people required an interpreter if they were to receive the presumed content of the speech (see LN 33.3).

s.d: an utterance having the form of language but requiring an inspired interpreter for an understanding of the content
s.c: Most scholars assume that the phenomena described in ⟦Acts 2:4|Acts 2:4⟧ (see LN 33.2) and in ⟦1 Corinthians 14:2|1 Corinthians 14:2⟧ are significantly different in that in one instance people understood in their own regional language or dialect and in the other instance an interpreter was required. It is for that reason that many interpret γλῶσσα in ⟦1 Corinthians 14:2|1 Corinthians 14:2⟧ as ecstatic speech, which was also an element in Hellenistic religions and constituted a symbol of divine inspiration.

s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:γλῶσσα<SDBG:γλῶσσα:000000>}[a] ‘tongue,’ {D:8.21}) to communicate orally
(figurative extension of meaning of {L:γλῶσσα<SDBG:γλῶσσα:000000>}[a] ‘tongue,’ {D:8.21}) the faculty or capacity for speech
s.c: In ⟦Luke 1:64|Luke 1:64⟧ στόμα and γλῶσσα appear to have the same referent and therefore may be regarded as essentially synonymous.

s.d: that which has been spoken or uttered
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:γλῶσσα<SDBG:γλῶσσα:000000>}[a] ‘tongue,’ {D:8.21}) a person as one who utters something{N:001}
a box in which money was kept
s.c: It may be useful, however, in rendering ⟦John 13:29|John 13:29⟧ to say simply ‘Judas had charge of the money’ or ‘Judas was the treasurer of the group,’ since the Greek expression may be understood as an idiom.

s.d: one who cards, cleans, and/or bleaches cloth
s.c: In ⟦Mark 9:3|Mark 9:3⟧ the reference is obviously to the process of bleaching, but a γναφεύς also was engaged in the cleaning of cloth as well as carding it, a process by which the nap of cloth was somewhat raised and made soft by being combed with bristles.

s.d: pertaining to possessing purported good character or quality
pertaining to possessing purported good character or quality
a condition resulting from the partial or complete absence of light (see {D:14.36})
s.c: In a number of languages it is impossible to speak of ‘darkness’ as being an agent in the sense of ⟦Luke 23:44|Luke 23:44⟧ ‘darkness covered the whole country.’ Accordingly, one must say ‘throughout the whole country it was dark’ or ‘it darkened over the whole country.’ In some languages darkness may be characterized as being a quality of the night, for example, ‘it was like night.’

s.dp: Think › To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
s.d: that which is purposed or intended, with the implication of judgment or resolve

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Have an Opinion, Hold a View
s.d: that which is regarded or considered to be the case
s.c: It is also possible to under stand γνώμη in ⟦Philemon 1:14|Philemon 1:14⟧ as ‘agreement’ or ‘consent’ (see LN 31.14).

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Agree, Consent
s.d: agreement based on knowledge
s.c: This interpretation of γνώμη in ⟦Philemon 1:14|Philemon 1:14⟧ is less likely than the meaning of γνώμη as ‘opinion’ (see LN 31.3).

s.d: to possess information about
s.g: to know; to know about; to have knowledge of; to be acquainted with; acquaintance

s.d: to cause information to be known by someone
possessing information about
the content of what is known
esoteric knowledge (primarily philosophical and religious), with the implication of its being heretical and contrary to the gospel
s.c: In ⟦1 Timothy 6:20|1 Timothy 6:20⟧, ψευδωνύμου γνώσεως may be rendered as ‘that which is falsely called knowledge’ or ‘knowledge which people think is true but is really false.’

s.d: coming to an understanding as the result of ability to experience and learn{N:001}
(derivative of {L:γινώσκω<SDBG:γινώσκω:000000>}[a] ‘to know,’ {D:28.1}) one who knows, with the usual implication of to know well
pertaining to that which is known

s.dp: Know › Well Known, Clearly Shown, Revealed
s.d: pertaining to being well known or well acquainted with
s.c: It may also be possible to understand γνωστός in ⟦Luke 2:44|Luke 2:44⟧ as meaning ‘friend’ (see LN 34.17).

s.dp: Know › Well Known, Clearly Shown, Revealed
s.d: pertaining to being well known or famous because of some outstanding quality
s.c: For another interpretation of γνωστός in ⟦Acts 4:16|Acts 4:16⟧, see γνωστός LN 58.55.

s.d: pertaining to being able to be known
s.g: what can be known; what is evident; what can be clearly seen
s.c: In a number of languages the phrase ‘can be known,’ expressing a capacity relating to a passive state, must be restructured in an active form. This may often be done by rendering ⟦Romans 1:19|Romans 1:19⟧ as ‘because what people can know about God is clearly evident to these persons’ or ‘they can clearly comprehend what they can know about God’ or ‘because they can clearly see what people can know about God.’

s.d: pertaining to being a friend or acquaintance of someone, and thus enjoying certain privileges as a result of such a relation
s.c: It is clear that in ⟦John 18:15|John 18:15⟧ γνωστός implies much more than simply being ‘well known by.’ To have been simply well known by the High Priest could have been a source of danger for the disciple. It was the fact of a relationship of friendship which made it possible for the disciple to view the proceedings.

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Unusual, Different From the Ordinary
s.d: pertaining to that which is unusual in the sense of being extraordinary
s.c: For another interpretation of γνωστός in ⟦Acts 4:16|Acts 4:16⟧, see γνωστός LN 28.32.

s.d: to express one’s discontent
to express one’s discontent
s.c: In a number of languages it may be necessary to restructure ‘complaint’ as a verb rather than as a noun, and therefore this expression in ⟦Acts 6:1|Acts 6:1⟧ may be rendered as ‘Greek-speaking Jews complained against what the local Jews were doing.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:γογγύζω<SDBG:γογγύζω:000000>} ‘to complain,’ {D:33.382}) one who has a habit of complaining or grumbling

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Hypocrisy, Pretense
s.d: one who habitually fools or deceives people through pretense

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: the Aramaic name of a hill near Jerusalem where executions took place; see also {D:8.11}

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city located at the southern part of the Dead Sea and destroyed because of its evil
(derivative of γέμω ‘to be laden,’ not occurring in the NT) a relatively heavy object which is carried
s.g: load; burden; cargo (as of a ship)

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: biological or legal parents

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: central hinge joint of the leg where the thigh is joined to the lower leg
s.c: In ⟦Luke 5:8|Luke 5:8⟧ the phrase ‘fell on his knees before Jesus’ should normally not be rendered literally since it might imply accidental stumbling. A more satisfactory equivalent may be ‘knelt down before,’ as a sign of worship or gratitude.|The term γόνυ occurs in a number of idiomatic phrases in the NT. For example, in ⟦Hebrews 12:12|Hebrews 12:12⟧ the command ‘to strengthen the weak knees’ should normally not be translated literally, but by an expression meaning ‘to strengthen determination’ or ‘to give courage to’ (see LN 25.152). The ‘bending of the knees’ in ⟦Mark 15:19|Mark 15:19⟧ was a sign of mock respect, and in such a context the term for ‘knee’ is often semantically absorbed into an expression meaning literally ‘bow down before’ (see LN 53.61).

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:γόνυ<SDBG:γόνυ:000000>}[a] ‘knee,’ {D:8.47}) a person in the attitude or position of one worshiping or submitting to authority{N:001}
(a Semitic idiom, literally: the knee bends, or: the knee bows) to bend or bow the knee as a symbol of religious devotion{N:002}
(an idiom, literally: straighten paralyzed knees) to gain encouragement by a strong resolve
s.g: to become encouraged; to encourage oneself by determination
s.c: See discussion at LN 23.170.

s.dp: Stances and Events Related to Stances › Kneel
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to place the knees, a Latinism) to kneel down before, with the implication of an act of reverence or of supplication
s.c: In a number of cultures, kneeling does not imply either reverence or an act of supplication. In some instances translators have used a functional substitute involving a similar type of stance, namely, ‘to bow low before,’ but it may be necessary to use a more or less literal description of ‘kneeling before’ and then to place in a marginal note an indication of the implications of such an act.

s.dp: Stances and Events Related to Stances › Kneel
s.d: to kneel down before, with the implication of an act of reverence or of supplication
s.c: In a number of cultures, kneeling does not imply either reverence or an act of supplication. In some instances translators have used a functional substitute involving a similar type of stance, namely, ‘to bow low before,’ but it may be necessary to use a more or less literal description of ‘kneeling before’ and then to place in a marginal note an indication of the implications of such an act.

s.d: a letter of the Greek alphabet{N:001}
any kind of written document, whether in book or manuscript form, with focus upon the content

s.dp: Artifacts › Instruments Used in Marking and Writing
s.d: an object containing writing addressed to one or more persons, normally written on papyrus{N:002}
s.c: In some languages it may be necessary to try to distinguish between a letter as an object and a letter as content or message. In ⟦Acts 23:33|Acts 23:33⟧ the focus seems to be upon the letter as an object, not necessarily upon the contents of the document. In most contexts, however, it is impossible to distinguish between a letter as a material object and a letter as a message (see LN 33.48).

s.d: a written statement of financial accounts, especially of debts
s.c: In place of the expression ‘here is your account,’ one may say ‘here is a list of what you owe.’

s.d: (pl; των n) the body of information acquired in school or from the study of writings
s.c: For a discussion of problems involved in translating ⟦John 7:15|John 7:15⟧, see μανθάνω (LN 27.12).

s.d: a recognized expert in Jewish law (including both canonical and traditional laws and regulations)
s.g: one who is learned in the Law; expert in the Law; expert in the Law of Moses

s.d: a person who has acquired a high level of education in a certain body of literature or discipline
s.c: In traditional translations γραμματεύς in contexts such as ⟦1 Corinthians 1:20|1 Corinthians 1:20⟧ and ⟦Matthew 13:52|Matthew 13:52⟧ has been rendered as ‘scribe,’ but this generally is misleading since the term ‘scribe’ is usually restricted in meaning to one who writes or copies documents. A γραμματεύς in Jewish life of Bible times would have been an expert in the Law or a scholar in the Holy Scriptures and not a mere copier of manuscripts.

s.d: a city official with responsibility for the records of a town or city and apparently certain responsibilities for maintaining law and order
pertaining to being written
a particular portion or unit of discourse{N:001}
s.g: passage; part of a document; part of Scripture
s.c: In rendering τόπος, περιοχή, or γραφή, it is often possible to use a rather general term such as the place or the part. In other instances one may wish to use a term meaning the words. Accordingly, ⟦Luke 4:21|Luke 4:21⟧ may be rendered as ‘these words have come true today as you have heard them being read.’

s.d: a particular passage of the OT{N:002}
(pl; ῶν f) the sacred writings of the OT
s.c: Some translators have mistakenly attempted to use the rendering ‘Bible’ when translating αἱ γραφαί ‘the Scriptures’ in the NT. The reference is to the OT and not to the entire Bible, including both New and Old Testaments. It is also a mistake to translate αἱ γραφαί as ‘God’s writings,’ for this would give the impression that God himself wrote the words.

s.d: to make the marks that form words on a surface (paper or other material), using a marking instrument (such as a pen)
s.c: Since the knowledge of writing is almost universal, there is usually no difficulty in obtaining a satisfactory term for writing. In some instances in which languages are only now being reduced to writing, a phrase is often employed, for example, ‘to make marks on paper’ or ‘to talk with lines’ or ‘to speak with paper.’

s.d: (pass. form of the verb) what is written, referring to Scripture
to write something down
s.c: It is possible to interpret καταγράφω in ⟦John 8:6|John 8:6⟧ as implying only the position of Jesus writing something down on the ground, but in view of the total context, one can also interpret it in the sense of writing down an accusation.

s.d: (derivative of γραῦς ‘old woman,’ not occurring in the NT) characteristic of old women
s.g: like old women say; like old women do

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sleep, Waking
s.d: to remain awake because of the need to continue alert
s.g: to stay awake; to be watchful
s.c: In some languages γρηγορέω in ⟦Matthew 24:43|Matthew 24:43⟧ may be rendered as ‘his eyes would be open’ or ‘he would surely see what was happening.’

s.dp: Learn › Be Ready To Learn, Pay Attention
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:γρηγορέω<SDBG:γρηγορέω:000000>}[a] ‘to stay awake,’ {D:23.72}) to be in continuous readiness and alertness to learn
s.g: to be alert; to be watchful; to be vigilant

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:γρηγορέω<SDBG:γρηγορέω:000000>}[a] ‘to stay awake,’ {D:23.72}) to remain fully alive and alert
s.g: to remain alive; to be alive

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Self-Control, Lack of Self-Control
s.d: to control oneself by thorough discipline
s.g: to discipline oneself; to keep oneself disciplined
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to discipline oneself’ is literally ‘to make oneself obey.’ This may sometimes be expressed idiomatically as ‘to command one’s heart.’

s.d: to experience vigorous training and control, with the implication of increased physical and/or moral strength
s.c: In rendering γυμνάζω in ⟦Hebrews 12:11|Hebrews 12:11⟧ it may be important in some languages to translate ‘those who have learned by such punishment’ or ‘those whose ways have been made right by such punishment’ or ‘those who because of punishment have learned how they must act.’

s.d: to engage in physical exercise as a way of improving the body
to dress in worn-out, ragged clothing
s.g: to wear ragged clothing; to wear rags; to be poorly clothed

s.d: pertaining to wearing no clothing or being very scantily clothed
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:γυμνός<SDBG:γυμνός:000000>}[a] ‘naked,’ {D:49.22}) easily able to be known in view of the fact that nothing is hidden
s.c: It is rare that one can employ in translating γυμνός b a term which literally means ‘naked,’ but it is possible to retain something of the metaphorical value by using a phrase such as ‘with nothing to cover’ or ‘with nothing which can be used to hide.’

s.d: the state of being naked or only scantily clothed
s.c: In the context of ⟦Romans 8:35|Romans 8:35⟧ ‘nakedness’ refers to poverty.

s.d: (a diminutive, pejorative derivative of {L:γυνή<SDBG:γυνή:000000>}[a] ‘woman,’ {D:9.34}) an adult woman of foolish and/or frivolous charter
(derivative of {L:γυνή<SDBG:γυνή:000000>}[a] ‘woman,’ {D:9.34}) pertaining to being a woman
an adult female person of marriageable age
s.c: In some languages it may be awkward to speak of ‘arresting men and women,’ since it is normal in such languages to speak of ‘men and women’ simply as ‘people.’ However, where the distinction of ‘men and women’ can be employed, it should be done, since the arresting of women for presumed heresy in NT times would seem far less justified than the arresting of men, who were supposed to take a more active part in new movements and thus were more likely to be arraigned before authorities.|As a form of address, γυνή was used in Koine Greek in speaking politely to a female person: ὦ γύναι, μεγάλη σου ἡ πίστις ‘Lady, your faith is great’ ⟦Matthew 15:28|Matthew 15:28⟧. In ⟦John 2:4|John 2:4⟧ Jesus uses γυνή to address his mother courteously.|In a number of languages it would be totally impossible to have Jesus address his mother merely as ‘woman.’ To do so in some languages would imply that Jesus was denying that Mary was his mother. In other languages, such an expression would imply that Jesus was calling his mother a prostitute or evil person. Accordingly, in a number of languages there is simply no other way in which Jesus could address his mother than as ‘mother’ or ‘my mother.’

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Based upon Marriage
s.d: a woman who is married to a man
s.c: The distinctions in meaning of γυνή woman (LN 9.34) and γυνή wife parallel those involving ἀνήρ and ἄνθρωπος (see LN 10.53). A number of languages, however, employ essentially the same usage as Greek in that a wife is simply called his woman, my woman, etc. The contexts normally indicate clearly which meaning of γυνή is involved.

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to touch a woman) to marry a woman
s.c: It is important to note that this expression in the second part of ⟦1 Corinthians 7:1|1 Corinthians 7:1⟧ may be either a statement by Paul or a quotation from a letter from the church of Corinth. This fact should be clearly noted in the margin.

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to take a woman) to marry a woman
(an idiom, literally: to have a woman) to be married to a woman

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a cryptic name to designate an enemy to be conquered by the Messiah
the corner of an area or construction, either an inside corner or an outside corner

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: (derivative of {L:δαιμόνιον<SDBG:δαιμόνιον:000000>}[a] ‘demon,’ {D:12.37}) to be possessed by a demon
s.c: In a number of languages one cannot speak of a person ‘being possessed by a demon.’ A more appropriate expression may be ‘the person possesses a demon.’ In other instances an idiomatic phrase is employed, ‘the demon rides the person’ or ‘the demon commands the person’ or even ‘the demon is the person.’

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: an evil supernatural being or spirit
s.c: While in a number of languages the Devil may be spoken of as ‘the chief of the demons,’ sometimes the demons are simply called ‘the spirits of the Devil’ or ‘the servants of the Devil.’|In a number of languages the difficulty in terminology for demons is not the absence of a term, but the abundance of different terms for different kinds of demons, each one of which may be responsible for particular kinds of human behavior, for example, insanity, depression, epilepsy, sex perversion, and violent assault. Sometimes demons are classified as ‘those of the home’ and ‘those of the forest,’ in which case the latter are normally regarded as more violent and virulent. When there is an abundance of different terms for demons and no generic term for all types of demons, one can usually select a class of demons which parallels most closely the descriptions of demon activity in the NT and use such a term with appropriate contextual qualifications so as to suggest that such a term is to be understood in a general sense.

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: a supernatural being of somewhat lesser status than {L:θεός<SDBG:θεός:000001>}[b] ‘god’ ({D:12.22})
s.c: The expression ‘foreign gods’ (⟦Acts 17:18|Acts 17:18⟧) may be rendered as ‘gods whom the foreigners worshiped’ or ‘gods of the foreigners.’ It would be wrong to render ‘foreign gods’ by a phrase which would mean ‘the gods are foreigners.’

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: (derivative of {L:δαιμόνιον<SDBG:δαιμόνιον:000000>}[a] ‘demon,’ {D:12.37}) pertaining to a demon
s.c: In some languages δαιμονιώδης may be rendered as ‘typical of the way a demon acts’ or ‘the way in which demons behave.’

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: an evil supernatural being or spirit
s.c: While in a number of languages the Devil may be spoken of as ‘the chief of the demons,’ sometimes the demons are simply called ‘the spirits of the Devil’ or ‘the servants of the Devil.’|In a number of languages the difficulty in terminology for demons is not the absence of a term, but the abundance of different terms for different kinds of demons, each one of which may be responsible for particular kinds of human behavior, for example, insanity, depression, epilepsy, sex perversion, and violent assault. Sometimes demons are classified as ‘those of the home’ and ‘those of the forest,’ in which case the latter are normally regarded as more violent and virulent. When there is an abundance of different terms for demons and no generic term for all types of demons, one can usually select a class of demons which parallels most closely the descriptions of demon activity in the NT and use such a term with appropriate contextual qualifications so as to suggest that such a term is to be understood in a general sense.

s.dp: Violence, Harm, Destroy, Kill › Harm, Wound
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of δάκνω ‘to bite,’ not occurring in the NT) to cause personal harm to someone

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Physiological Products of the Body
s.d: the watery fluid which flows from the eye

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Laugh, Cry, Groan
s.d: to weep, with the clear implication of shedding tears
s.c: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between weeping which results from sorrow and grief and weeping caused by physical suffering. Without careful attention to such a distinction, a translator may seriously distort the meaning of the text.

s.d: a ring for the finger, normally made of gold or silver and usually containing the signet of the owner by which he could mark ownership and seal documents

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: one of the five long and slender projections of the human hand, used for writing, pointing, grasping, and other activities
s.c: Though it may seem quite logical to speak of ‘writing with the finger’ (⟦John 8:6|John 8:6⟧), in some languages one is required to speak of ‘writing with the hand.’ Similarly, in ⟦Matthew 23:4|Matthew 23:4⟧ the idiom ‘to lift a finger’ is more satisfactorily expressed as ‘to lift a hand.’ Expressions such as ‘to lift the hand’ and ‘to lift the finger’ must be carefully studied for their idiomatic significance, for ‘to lift the hand’ may mean ‘to release something,’ while ‘to lift the finger’ may be a lewd gesture.|In a number of languages the expression ‘to lift a finger’ (⟦Matthew 23:4|Matthew 23:4⟧) may be best rendered as ‘to do a thing to help’ or ‘to help in any way.’ For δάκτυλος θεοῦ ‘the finger of God’ (⟦Luke 11:20|Luke 11:20⟧), see LN 76.3.

s.d: power as an expression of the activity of a person or supernatural being{N:001}
s.c: In some languages there is no abstract term for ‘power.’ The equivalent of doing something by the power of someone is ‘someone makes it possible to do’ or, in a figurative sense, ‘someone gives strength to do.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a place of uncertain location near the western shore of the Lake of Galilee

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: the southern part of Illyricum
to bring under control and to continue to restrain
s.g: to control; to bring under control; to hold in check
s.c: In many languages it may be difficult to speak of ‘bringing a person under control.’ It may therefore be more appropriate to use some such phrase as ‘not allow a person to do just what he wants’ or ‘make a person behave’ or ‘make a person obey.’ In speaking of animals, one may render ⟦James 3:7|James 3:7⟧ as ‘all kinds of wild animals … can be made to obey a person.’

s.d: the young female of cattle
s.c: A δάμαλις ‘heifer’ would be older and bigger than a calf but younger than a cow, since ‘heifer’ refers to a cow before she has been impregnated or given birth to her first calf.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: an Athenian woman converted by Paul

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of {L:Δαμασκός<SDBG:Δαμασκός:000000>} ‘Damascus,’ {D:93.459}) a person who lives in or is a native of Damascus

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: the capital of Syria

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Lend, Loan, Interest, Borrow, Bank
s.d: (derivative of δανείζω ‘to lend money,’ {D:57.209}) that which has been loaned

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Lend, Loan, Interest, Borrow, Bank
s.d: to lend money, normally with the expectation of receiving the same amount in return plus interest
s.g: to make a loan; to lend money
s.c: In ⟦Luke 6:34|Luke 6:34⟧ it is possible that no interest payment is involved, in which case the meaning is similar to that of κίχρημι ‘to lend’ (LN 57.214).

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Lend, Loan, Interest, Borrow, Bank
s.d: to borrow money, normally with the implication of interest to be paid
s.c: It is possible, however, that in ⟦Matthew 5:42|Matthew 5:42⟧ interest on the loan is not involved.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a major OT prophet

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Lend, Loan, Interest, Borrow, Bank
s.d: (derivative of δανείζω ‘to lend money,’ {D:57.209}) a person whose business it is to lend money to others at an interest rate
to pay out money (or other assets) as a means of obtaining benefits or in payment for benefits
s.g: to spend; to pay out; to pay expenses
s.c: For another interpretation of δαπανάω in ⟦2 Corinthians 12:15|2 Corinthians 12:15⟧, see δαπανάω LN 42.27.

s.d: to spend completely, with the implication of uselessly, and therefore, to waste
s.c: In some languages ‘to waste’ may be expressed as ‘to use up and to get no benefit’ or ‘to have, but for no purpose.’

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:δαπανάω<SDBG:δαπανάω:000000>}[a] ‘‘to spend,’ {D:57.146}) to exert great effort in doing something
s.g: to do anything; to exert great effort
s.c: It is possible, however, that δαπανάω in ⟦2 Corinthians 12:15|2 Corinthians 12:15⟧ should be understood in the literal sense and hence rendered ‘I will be glad to spend all I have on your behalf’ (see δαπανάω LN 57.146).

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Pay, Price, Cost
s.d: (derivative of {L:δαπανάω<SDBG:δαπανάω:000000>}[a] ‘to spend,’ {D:57.146}) the amount spent or to be spent in procuring some object or benefit

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a king of Israel and an ancestor in the genealogy of Jesus
a marker of an additive relation, but with the possible implication of some contrast
marker of a sequence of closely related events
a marker of contrast
a marker of two or more items which are additively related and thematically parallel
a marker of sets of items in contrast with one another
s.g: on the one hand … but on the other hand

s.d: (derivative of {L:δέομαι<SDBG:δέομαι:000000>} ‘to plead, to beg,’ {D:33.170}) that which is asked with urgency based on presumed need{N:001}
to be that which must necessarily take place, often with the implication of inevitability
s.c: It is impossible to tell in a context such as ⟦Mark 13:7|Mark 13:7⟧ whether δεῖ implies mere inevitability of an event or whether the events are somehow part of the plan and purpose of God. The latter interpretation could only be derived from broader theological implications and not from the meaning of δεῖ itself.

s.d: to be something which should be done as the result of compulsion, whether internal (as a matter of duty) or external (law, custom, and circumstances)
s.g: should; ought; to have to do

s.dp: Know › Well Known, Clearly Shown, Revealed
s.d: (derivative of {L:δείκνυμι<SDBG:δείκνυμι:000000>}[a] ‘to make known,’ {D:28.47}) the means by which the nature of something is made known, particularly as an example of what is to be avoided
s.g: example (such as to warn); means by which something is known

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Shame, Disgrace, Humiliation
s.d: to cause someone to suffer public disgrace or shame
s.g: to disgrace in public; to put to shame
s.c: The expression ‘to disgrace in public’ may be rendered in some languages as ‘to cause everyone to think bad about’ or ‘to cause everyone to speak in whispers about.’

s.dp: Know › Well Known, Clearly Shown, Revealed
s.d: to make known the character or significance of something by visual, auditory, gestural, or linguistic means{N:001}
s.g: to make known; to demonstrate; to show
s.c: For another interpretation of δείκνυμι in ⟦1 Corinthians 12:31|1 Corinthians 12:31⟧, see δείκνυμι LN 33.150.

s.d: to explain the meaning or significance of something by demonstration{N:002}
s.g: to show; to explain; to make clear
s.c: For another interpretation of δείκνυμι in ⟦1 Corinthians 12:31|1 Corinthians 12:31⟧, see δείκνυμι LN 28.47.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Fear, Terror, Alarm
s.d: a state of fear because of a lack of courage or moral strength
s.c: ‘Cowardice’ is often rendered by means of an idiom, for example, ‘to have a fallen heart,’ ‘to have a soft heart,’ or ‘one’s heart has disappeared.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Fear, Terror, Alarm
s.d: to be fearful and cowardly
s.g: to be cowardly; to lack courage

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Fear, Terror, Alarm
s.d: pertaining to being cowardly
s.c: In some languages a ‘coward’ is ‘one who always runs’ or ‘one who runs away at nothing.’

s.dp: Discourse Referentials › Whom or What Spoken or Written About
s.d: a reference to an entity which one cannot or does not wish to make explicit (in the NT only a reference to a man)
s.c: Though in many translations δεῖνα is translated as ‘certain,’ this can give a wrong impression since it would imply that the individual is known to the parties involved or has been identified by the context.

s.d: an extreme point on a scale involving negative values

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: to eat a meal, without reference to any particular time of the day or to the type of food involved
s.g: to eat a meal; to have a meal
s.c: In some languages it is impossible to speak of ‘having a meal’ without indicating the time of day or the nature of the food consumed.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: a meal whether simple or elaborate (this generic meaning of δεῖπνον is in contrast with the more specific meaning of δεῖπνον[b], {D:23.25})
s.g: a meal; a banquet; a feast
s.c: Though ἄριστον, δεῖπνον, and βρῶσις are highly generic in this usage, it is not necessary to translate these terms by a corresponding generic term in another language, since a more specific term may fit the context more satisfactorily. In fact, a generic term might be quite inappropriate in that it would suggest in the case of ⟦Mark 6:21|Mark 6:21⟧ that Herod was quite stingy in simply providing an ordinary meal for his officials.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: the principal meal of the day, usually in the evening
s.c: Though in the so-called Western world there is a tendency to have three meals each day, breakfast, lunch, and dinner (or supper), in many parts of the world there are only two principal meals: one eaten around nine or ten o’clock in the morning, and another at four or five o’clock in the afternoon.|In some languages there is a very important distinction made between a more or less formal meal and the relatively informal times of eating which might be called ‘snacks.’ These would be occasions on which one would eat only one kind of food and possibly in relatively small quantities.

s.d: an elaborate meal
a set of beliefs concerning deity, with the implication of corresponding behavior
pertaining to being religious
s.c: δεισιδαίμων may occur in either a good or a bad sense; that is to say, it may mean either ‘very religious’ or ‘superstitious,’ although the meaning of ‘superstitious’ is primarily a later development in the meaning of this word. In ⟦Acts 17:22|Acts 17:22⟧ there seems every reason to believe that Paul was using the term in a positive sense.

s.d: cardinal number, where there are ten instances of a countable entity
cardinal number, where there are fifteen instances of a countable entity

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a league of ten cities in a region east of the Jordan
cardinal number, where there are fourteen instances of a countable entity
s.c: It is possible that δεκατέσσαρες in ⟦Matthew 1:17|Matthew 1:17⟧ has a symbolic meaning in view of its being equivalent to twice seven. Others have suggested that the number fourteen is derived from the value of the name David based on the numerical values of the consonants in the Hebrew form of the name. This may explain certain of the irregularities in the listing of the generations.

s.d: tenth in a series involving either time, space, or set
a tenth part of an object, series, or mass
s.c: In rendering ‘the tenth of the city fell’ in ⟦Revelation 11:13|Revelation 11:13⟧, it may be necessary in some languages to say ‘for every ten buildings, one building fell’ or ‘every tenth building in the city collapsed.’

s.d: (semantic derivative of {L:δέκατος<SDBG:δέκατος:000001>}[b] ‘tenth part,’ {D:60.65}) a tenth of a substance being offered for some distinctive purpose
to cause someone to pay a tenth
s.g: to collect tithes; to exact tithes from
s.c: In a number of languages there are problems involved in speaking of ‘a tenth,’ and accordingly there are difficulties in formulating expressions about ‘tithing.’ In some languages one may speak of ‘a tenth’ as ‘one part of ten parts’ or ‘one part together with nine parts.’ ‘To tithe’ may be rendered as ‘from ten parts to pay one part’ or ‘to pay one part and to keep nine parts.’

s.d: to give a tenth of one’s income
s.g: to give a tenth; to tithe
s.c: In ⟦Hebrews 7:9|Hebrews 7:9⟧ it may be important to indicate clearly that it was not Levi himself who received the tenth but his descendants. Therefore, one may render the latter part of ⟦Hebrews 7:9|Hebrews 7:9⟧ as ‘Levi, whose descendants collect the tenth, also paid it.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With
s.d: pertaining to that which is pleasing in view of its being acceptable
s.c: In a number of languages it is necessary to restructure expressions containing ‘acceptable to’ or ‘pleasing to.’ For example, in ⟦Acts 10:35|Acts 10:35⟧ it may be necessary to translate ‘God accepts whoever worships him and does what is right’ or ‘God is pleased with whoever worships him and does what is right.’ Similarly, in ⟦1 Timothy 2:3|1 Timothy 2:3⟧ one may translate ‘this is good, and God our Savior likes it’ or ‘… is happy because of it.’

s.d: pertaining to being welcomed or acceptable
s.g: one who is welcomed; one who is acceptable
s.c: In rendering this expression in ⟦Luke 4:24|Luke 4:24⟧ it may be necessary to restructure the relationships somewhat radically, for example, ‘because people of a town do not wish to accept one of their fellow townsmen as a prophet.’

s.d: pertaining to being appropriate or fitting, with the implication of being favorable

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Sin, Wrongdoing, Guilt
s.d: to lure or entice someone to sin (compare δέλεαρ ‘bait,’ not occurring in the NT)
s.g: to lead astray; to lure into sin
s.c: δελεάζω may often be translated as ‘to make sinning look attractive’ or ‘to make sin taste good’ or ‘to wave sin in front of a person’s nose.’

s.d: any kind of relatively large woody plant
s.c: In rendering δένδρον ‘tree’ it is important in a number of contexts to determine whether or not the trees in question produce edible fruit, since in a number of languages this distinction is reflected in the use of quite different terms.

s.d: exact meaning unsure; a soldier other than heavily armed infantry or horsemen
s.g: foot soldier; lightly armed soldier; spearman

s.dp: Spacial Orientations › Left, Right, Straight Ahead, Opposite
s.d: pertaining to being to the right of some point of reference
s.c: For another interpretation of δεξιός as part of an idiom in ⟦Mark 10:37|Mark 10:37⟧, see LN 87.34.

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: an abbreviated reference to a person’s right hand, which is generally the dominant hand; positive associations as opposed to the left
s.c: The expression in ⟦Matthew 6:3|Matthew 6:3⟧ is idiomatic and means not letting others know about the good which one does (see LN 28.74). The right hand is often spoken of idiomatically as ‘the good hand’ or ‘the strong hand.’ Sometimes it is called ‘the mouth hand,’ that is to say, the hand which one uses in eating.|For δεξιά in the idiom δεξιὰς δίδωμι ‘to give the right hand’ (⟦Galatians 2:9|Galatians 2:9⟧), see LN 34.42.

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:δεξιός<SDBG:δεξιός:000001>}[b] ‘right hand,’ {D:8.32}) power, with the added implication of authority

s.dp: Association › Establish or Confirm a Relation
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to give right hands) to acknowledge an agreement establishing some relation, normally involving the actual practice of shaking hands
s.g: to make a covenant; to make an agreement

s.d: to ask for with urgency, with the implication of presumed need

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of {L:Δέρβη<SDBG:Δέρβη:000000>} ‘Derbe,’ {D:93.462}) a person who lives in or is a native of Derbe

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city in Lycaonia

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: skin of an animal, normally including attached hair and sometimes tanned
s.c: In a number of languages it is important to distinguish clearly between tanned and untanned skins or hides. Furthermore, one must often make a distinction between a skin which still has the hair on it and that which does not. In ⟦Hebrews 11:37|Hebrews 11:37⟧ the likelihood is that these skins were tanned and still retained the hair as extra protection.

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: (derivative of {L:δέρμα<SDBG:δέρμα:000000>} ‘skin,’ {D:6.184}) pertaining to being made of skin or leather
to strike or beat repeatedly
s.g: to strike; to beat; to whip

s.d: to bind or tie on
s.c: Note, however, that the context of ⟦Matthew 23:4|Matthew 23:4⟧ is figurative.

s.d: (derivative of {L:δεσμεύω<SDBG:δεσμεύω:000000>} ‘to bind,’ {D:18.15}) that which has been tied up or tied together
(derivative of {L:δεσμός<SDBG:δεσμός:000001>}[b] ‘to be in prison,’ {D:37.115}) a person who is under custody in prison

s.dp: Artifacts › Instruments Used in Binding and Fastening
s.d: any instrument or means of binding or tying; used for binding objects together or restraining prisoners
s.c: In translating ⟦Acts 16:26|Acts 16:26⟧ one may often use a descriptive phrase, for example, ‘those things that bound them’ or ‘things with which they were tied.’ It is generally more satisfactory, however, to employ wherever possible a more specific referent, for example, ‘ropes,’ ‘chains’ or ‘fetters.’

s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:δεσμός<SDBG:δεσμός:000000>}[a] ‘bonds,’ {D:6.14}) the state of being in prison
s.c: The state of being a prisoner is often expressed somewhat idiomatically, for example, ‘to be tied hand and foot,’ ‘to be chained like a dog,’ or ‘to look through iron bars.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:δεσμός<SDBG:δεσμός:000000>}[a] ‘bond,’ {D:6.14}) a state of physical incapacity or illness, usually as the result of some controlling supernatural force (in {S:04201301600040}, the result of the activity of Satan)
